summary: Extends WebDAV so clients can create redirect reference resources: items on a server whose normal answer is an HTTP 3xx redirect to somewhere else. This lets a target be reached indirectly through another address. It makes no integrity guarantees. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Like a signpost you can put up in a folder that says, the thing you want has moved, go over there. Visitors get sent along automatically.

subtitle: Signposts on a server that point clients to resources elsewhere.

tldr.problem: Web storage systems (WebDAV) need a way to create shortcut paths to existing resources without copying them, so a resource can be accessed from multiple locations in a folder hierarchy.
tldr.mechanism: Redirect reference resources are special WebDAV items that respond to requests with HTTP 3xx redirects pointing to a target resource elsewhere.
tldr.outcome: Clients can now create alternative access paths to shared resources, solving the problem of resources that logically belong in multiple collections.

today: RFC 4437 is an Experimental specification for WebDAV redirect references. It is not widely deployed but defines a mechanism for servers that choose to support alternative resource paths.

sections.title: Redirect Reference Resources
sections.content:
This RFC extends WebDAV (Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning) to let clients create redirect reference resources: special items that redirect requests to other resources. WebDAV organizes HTTP resources into folder-like collections, but this hierarchy forces each resource into a single location, even when a resource logically belongs in multiple categories.

A redirect reference solves this problem by creating an alternative path. Instead of copying a resource, you create a small placeholder that says where the real resource lives. Requests to the placeholder get a redirect response (HTTP 3xx) pointing to the actual resource.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a document could fit in many folders. Instead of keeping copies everywhere, you put up a sign in each folder that points to the real copy.

sections.title: How Redirect References Work
sections.content:
A redirect reference is a resource with properties but no body (no content). When a client requests a redirect reference with any method, the default response is HTTP 302 (Found) accompanied by a Location header containing the target resource's URI, along with a new Redirect-Ref response header.

Non-aware clients automatically follow the redirect to the target. Aware clients can either follow the redirect or query the reference resource's DAV:reftarget property to learn the target URI directly. The Apply-To-Redirect-Ref request header (set to 'T') lets aware clients operate on the redirect reference itself rather than following the redirect.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask for the signpost, the server says 'go over there' and gives you the address. You can either go there, or ask the signpost what address it holds.

sections.title: Creating and Updating Redirects
sections.content:
The MKREDIRECTREF method creates a redirect reference resource by sending an XML body with the target URI and an optional redirect-lifetime value (permanent using HTTP 301, or temporary using HTTP 302). If creation succeeds, the server returns HTTP 201 (Created).

The UPDATEREDIRECTREF method updates an existing redirect reference to change its target or lifetime. The method body is an XML element that specifies which properties to update; unchanged properties are left alone.

Both methods are non-idempotent, so their responses must not be cached. If either request fails, the server must restore its previous state.
sections.plainLanguage: You use special commands (MKREDIRECTREF and UPDATEREDIRECTREF) to create or change signposts. If something goes wrong, the server puts everything back the way it was.

sections.title: Properties and Server Discovery
sections.content:
Every redirect reference resource has two required properties: DAV:reftarget (the target URI, read-only after creation) and DAV:redirect-lifetime (whether the redirect is permanent or temporary). Both are protected properties that servers manage.

The DAV:resourcetype property includes a DAV:redirectref element to mark the resource as a redirect. Clients discover redirect reference support by checking the DAV header in an OPTIONS response, which lists redirectrefs as a compliance class if the server supports the feature and the MKREDIRECTREF method if the location allows reference creation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each signpost has properties that say where it points and whether it is meant to be permanent or temporary. The server can tell you if it knows how to handle signposts.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
Redirect references inherit all security considerations from HTTP and WebDAV, but introduce new risks. A malicious actor could create redirect references on a trusted server to trick users into sending information to an untrusted system. Clients mitigate this by notifying users of redirects for requests other than GET or HEAD.

Redirect loops are possible if a reference points to another reference that points back, though servers can detect same-server loops. The references may also reveal private collection structures through the DAV:reftarget property, which any user with access to the reference can read. Property-level access control can restrict this visibility. There are no integrity guarantees: a redirect may point to a resource that no longer exists.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could put up fake signposts to trick you. The server tries to warn you when redirects happen. Signposts can also accidentally point in circles, or point to places that have gone away.
